ex-E103-1.title: Finding the distance to a star using parallax
ex-E103-1.question:
R Doradus, a star of radius 298R⊙, shows a maximum shift from position X to Y over one year relative to background stars as shown below.

(a) Estimate the distance to R Doradus.

(b) Estimate the angular size (in arcsec) of R Doradus in the sky.

Given: 1 pc = 3.09 × 1016 m, R⊙ = 6.96 × 108 m
ex-E103-1.answer:
(a) From the figure, the maximum angular shift of R Doradus is 0.036″.

Parallax p = 0.036″2 = 0.018″

Distance to R Doradus = 1p = 10.018 = 55.6 pc

(b) Angular size of R Doradus = 2 × 298 × 6.96 × 10855.6 × 3.09 × 1016

= 2.414 × 10−7 rad

= 2.414 × 10−7 rad × 180 × 3600″π

= 0.0498″

ex-E103-3.title: Relating magnitudes with luminosities and apparent brightness
ex-E103-3.question:
The following table lists the luminosities and apparent brightness of the Sun and the star Altair.

Star

Luminosity / W

Apparent brightness / W m−2

Sun

3.84 × 1026

1358

Altair

4.07 × 1027

1.29 × 10−8

(a) (i) Which of them gives out more energy into space per unit time? Explain.

(ii) Which of them looks brighter as observed from the Earth? Explain.

(b) Hence, compare their (i) absolute magnitudes and (ii) apparent magnitudes.
ex-E103-3.answer:
(a) (i) Since Altair has a greater luminosity, it gives out more energy into space per unit time.

(ii) Since the Sun has a higher apparent brightness, it looks brighter.

(b) (i) The absolute magnitude of Altair is smaller than that of the Sun.

(ii) The apparent magnitude of the Sun is smaller than that of Altair.

ex-E103-5.title: Sizes of stars
ex-E103-5.question: Arrange stars X, Y and Z in the figure below in ascending order of their sizes. Explain briefly.
ex-E103-5.answer:
From L ∝ R2T4, Z has the same surface temperature but a lower luminosity than Y, so Z has a smaller radius than Y.

While X has the same luminosity but a lower surface temperature than Y, so X has a larger radius than Y.

∴ Z < Y < X

ex-E103-6.title: Comparing Altair and the Sun
ex-E103-6.question:
Star Altair has a surface temperature of 7350 K and a luminosity of 10.6L⊙. The Sun is a class G star with a surface temperature of 5780 K.

(a) Deduce whether the spectral class of Altair is class A or M.

(b) Indicate the position of Altair relative to the Sun in an H-R diagram.

(c) Estimate the radius of Altair in terms of solar radius R⊙.

(d) Does Altair or the Sun give out more red light per unit surface area? Explain.
ex-E103-6.answer:
(a) Class A. As Altair has a higher surface temperature than the Sun.

(b) See the H-R diagram on the right. Altair is hotter than the Sun. It should be to the left of the Sun in the diagram. Also, Altair is more luminous than the Sun. Therefore, it should be at the upper left above the Sun.

(c) By LAL⊙=(RAR⊙)2(TAT⊙)4,

RA=LAL⊙×(T⊙TA)2R⊙=10.6×(57807350)2R⊙=2.01R⊙

(d) Altair gives out more red light per unit surface area than the Sun. Altair has a higher surface temperature, so it emits more radiation at all wavelengths including red light than the Sun.
ex-E103-6.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E103  |  Source PDF p. 30, 31

ex-E103-7.title: Doppler effect of a star
ex-E103-7.question:
We observe a line in the spectrum of a star with a wavelength of 600.1 nm. Laboratory measurements show that the line should have an unshifted wavelength of 600.0 nm.

(a) Find the radial velocity of the star. Take c = 3.00 × 108 m s−1.

(b) Deduce and explain whether the star is approaching or receding from the Earth.
ex-E103-7.answer:
(a) By Δλλ0 ≈ vrc,

radial velocity ≈ (Δλλ0)c = 600.1 – 600.0600.0 × 3.00 × 108 = 5 × 104 m s–1

(b) The positive sign for the radial velocity means that the star is moving away from the Earth.

Alternative solution:

The spectral line shifts to a longer wavelength. This indicates the star is moving away from the Earth.
ex-E103-7.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E103  |  Source PDF p. 36

ex-E103-8.title: The radial velocity curve of 51 Pegasi
ex-E103-8.question:
A planet is discovered to orbit the star 51 Pegasi. By measuring the Doppler shift, the radial velocity of 51 Pegasi as observed on Earth is deduced. The graph shows the change in radial velocity against time. It is known that the mass of 51 Pegasi is 2.10 × 1030 kg. Assume that we are looking along the orbital plane of 51 Pegasi and its planet, and their orbits are circular.

(a) Find the orbital periods and angular velocities of 51 Pegasi and its planet.

(b) Find the orbital speed and orbital radius of 51 Pegasi.

(c) Calculate the orbital radius and hence the orbital speed of the planet. Assume that the mass of 51 Pegasi is much larger than that of its planet.

Take G = 6.67 × 10−11 N m2 kg−2.
ex-E103-8.answer:
(a) Period of the planet = period of 51 Pegasi

= period of the radial velocity curve

= 4.23 days

51 Pegasi and its planet have the same angular velocity ω.

ω = 2πT = 2π4.23 × 24 × 3600 = 1.719 × 10–5 rad s–1 ≈ 1.72 × 10–5 rad s–1

(b) Orbital speed of 51 Pegasi = amplitude of the radial velocity curve = 60 m s−1

Let R be the orbital radius of 51 Pegasi.

By v = Rω,

R = vω = 601.719 × 10–5 = 3.49 × 106 m

(c) Let M and m be the masses of 51 Pegasi and its planet, r be the orbital radius of the planet. Assume R to be negligible as the mass of 51 Pegasi is much larger than that of its planet. Consider the gravitational pull between the star and the planet.

By GMmr2 = mrω2,

r=GMω23=(6.67×10−11)(2.10×1030)(1.719×10−5)23=7.79×109 m

∴ Orbital speed of the planet = rω = (7.79 × 109) × (1.719 × 10−5) = 1.34 × 105 m s−1

Exercise 3.4 Q8 (p.141)

ex-E103-9.title: Stars in a binary system
ex-E103-9.question:
Stars X and Y are suspected to be stars in a binary system. The radial velocity curves for the two stars are shown in Figure a. The maximum shift in wavelength of the spectral lines from X is shown in Figure b.

(a) State the evidence to support that X and Y are stars in a binary system.

(b) Refer to the radial velocity curve of X. Which moment does the maximum shift in the spectral lines shown in Figure b correspond to?

(c) The wavelength of the Hβ line obtained in a laboratory is 486.4 nm. What is the maximum Doppler shift of the line from X?

Take c = 3.00 × 108 m s−1.
ex-E103-9.answer:
(a) X and Y revolve with the same period in antiphase.

(b) At time = 12 hours.

(c) Maximum radial velocity of X = amplitude of curve X = 70 km s−1

By ∆λλ0 = vrc, ∆λ = (vrc) × λ0 = 70 × 1033.00 × 108 × 486.4 = 0.113 nm

The maximum Doppler shift of the Hβ line observed is 0.113 nm.
ex-E103-9.think:
Assume that the orbits of the stars are circular and the observer lies on the same orbital plane. Deduce the orbital radii and hence the masses of X and Y. Take G=6.67×10−11 N m2 kg−2.

Caution: Unlike an exoplanetary system, the stars in a binary system may be of comparable mass. The orbital radius of both stars must be considered in the calculation.
ex-E103-9.thinkAnswer:
From the radial-velocity graph, T=48 h=172 800 s, vX=70 km s−1 and vY=40 km s−1. Because the observer lies in the orbital plane, these amplitudes are the orbital speeds.

rX=vXT2π=(70×103)(172800)2π=1.93×109 m.

rY=vYT2π=(40×103)(172800)2π=1.10×109 m.

The separation is a=rX+rY=3.03×109 m. Gravity supplies the centripetal forces, giving MX+MY=4π2a3GT2=5.49×1029 kg (using unrounded radii).

The centre-of-mass condition is MXrX=MYrY, so MXMY=rYrX=47. Therefore MX=2.00×1029 kg and MY=3.49×1029 kg. Values are approximate because the speeds and period are read from the graph.
